frames.main_point: In practice, high-precision hydraulic motion is achieved using integrated actuator units that combine a piston, valves, and a position sensor under closed-loop control to regulate position.
frames.source_quote: AFAIK (I'm not in the field) high precision hydraulics are pre-packaged units of piston, valves and position sensor and control the piston for position.

frames.label: Hydraulic positioning’s disadvantages are only justified when very high force is required
frames.main_point: Hydraulic positioning’s disadvantages are only justified when very high force is required. Hobby‑scale CNC mill axes typically need little force, so electric screw or rack drives are a more suitable choice than hydraulics.
frames.source_quote: The distinction is that usually the down sides of hydraulic positioning are only worth it if you need a lot of force to complete the operation. In your case with a hobby-scale CNC mill all of your travel axes can operate on very little force.
frames.subject: hydraulic actuation suitability for CNC axes
frames.thread_title: Hydraulic linear actuators as CNC axis instead of screws

frames.label: High axis speeds with hydraulic cylinders are constrained by hose flow limits and the large oil volumes required
frames.main_point: High axis speeds with hydraulic cylinders are constrained by hose flow limits and the large oil volumes required. Matching screw or rack speeds would demand oversized pumps, hoses, and ports, driving up cost compared to stepper/servo drives.
frames.source_quote: even smallish hydraulic cylinders require a significant volume of oil, and there are practical limits on the flow speed inside of hoses, so moving enough oil to get a hydraulic cylinder moving as fast as a lead screw or rack and pinion can move would require a large pump, large hoses, and large ports. All of this is possible, but very expensive as compared to a simple stepper or servo motor.
frames.subject: hydraulic axis speed limited by oil volume and hose flow
frames.thread_title: Hydraulic linear actuators as CNC axis instead of screws

frames.label: Hydraulic valves inherently leak, so precision positioning requires compensating measures
frames.main_point: Hydraulic valves inherently leak, so precision positioning requires compensating measures. Achieving acceptable performance often entails high‑precision valves, counterbalance circuitry, and diligent seal maintenance, adding complexity and cost.
frames.source_quote: By there nature, pretty much all hydraulic valves involve some amount of leakage. Part of designing hydraulic systems is characterizing the amount of leakage and taking measures to compensate for it where the consequences are unacceptable. Again, it is possible to overcome these challenges, but buying high-precision valves, detailing counterbalance circuits, and maintaining the seals are all unnecessary costs.
frames.subject: hydraulic valve leakage and compensation needs
frames.thread_title: Hydraulic linear actuators as CNC axis instead of screws

frames.label: Because hydraulic valves are dynamic and nonlinear, precise positioning needs careful control tuning and robust feedback
frames.main_point: Because hydraulic valves are dynamic and nonlinear, precise positioning needs careful control tuning and robust feedback. In contrast, stepper or VFD-based electric drives are far easier to configure for accurate motion at the hobby-machine level.
frames.source_quote: Hydraulic valves have moving parts that take time and power to actuate. They don't have perfectly linear responses with respect to time, voltage, or pressure differentials. As a result, achieving precise position control requires more careful control tuning and feedback. By contrast, for a hobbyist level machine using stepper motors, you can pretty much treat this entire challenge as a solved problem. Even at a higher level, configuring a VFD and controlling its setpoints is much easier than controlling a hydraulic valve with feedback.
frames.subject: control complexity for hydraulic positioning
frames.thread_title: Hydraulic linear actuators as CNC axis instead of screws

frames.label: Hydraulic actuators tend to cost more than electric motors due to weaker economies of scale and higher manufacturing...
frames.main_point: Hydraulic actuators tend to cost more than electric motors due to weaker economies of scale and higher manufacturing demands. More precise machining, additional raw material, and tighter QC increase unit cost.
frames.source_quote: Hydraulic components are not produced in the same volumes that electric motors are, so there's not nearly as much of an economy of scale. In general hydraulic parts require more precise machining, more raw materials, and more detailed QC than motors, all of which translates into cost.
frames.subject: hydraulic component cost drivers vs electric motors
frames.thread_title: Hydraulic linear actuators as CNC axis instead of screws

frames.label: Hydraulic axes require at least two large, stiff hoses, making routing on moving machines cumbersome and failure clea...
frames.main_point: Hydraulic axes require at least two large, stiff hoses, making routing on moving machines cumbersome and failure cleanup messy. Electric motors only need a single cable for power/control, simplifying cable management.
frames.source_quote: Whereas an electric motor can be driven by one cable with power and control, hydraulic actuators need two hoses at a minimum for precise control in two directions. The hoses are much larger and stiffer than corresponding cables, and failures are more of a mess. When an actuator is being moved by another axis, the logistics of routing the hoses is a fairly big pain.
frames.subject: hydraulic hose routing complexity vs electrical cabling
frames.thread_title: Hydraulic linear actuators as CNC axis instead of screws

frames.label: Hydraulic systems are harder for typical users to diagnose and disassemble than electrical drives
frames.main_point: Hydraulic systems are harder for typical users to diagnose and disassemble than electrical drives. Troubleshooting hydraulics needs specialized gauges/fittings and disassembly risks messy fluid spills, whereas many electrical issues can be probed with a multimeter.
frames.source_quote: Most users are better equipped to service electrical equipment than hydraulic equipment. A simple multimeter can allow a wide range of diagnostics on electrical equipment, whereas one needs a fair number of gauges and fittings to really find a problem in a hydraulic circuit. Even more than that, hydraulics are harder to disassemble since pretty much everything is a pressure component and can create a big mess.
frames.subject: serviceability of hydraulics vs electrical systems
